title: Constraints, keyof, and Indexed Access
summary: Constrain type parameters so generic code can use their members, and type lookups exactly with keyof, indexed access, and const type parameters.
intro: A plain type parameter could be any type at all, so a generic function can't do much with its values. A constraint says what every `T` must have, like an `id` or a `length`, and callers still get back their own full type. In this lesson you add constraints, turn an object type's keys into a type with `keyof`, look up a property's type with `T[K]`, and steer inference with `const` type parameters and `NoInfer`. Together they are the patterns behind most typed helpers you'll read in libraries.

steps.title: Constraints

examples.title: The longer of two
examples.prompt: Pick the longer of two strings and the longer of two arrays with one generic `longest`, then use each result as its own type.
examples.explanation: Strings and arrays both have a numeric `length`, so both calls meet the constraint. Each call still infers its own `T`: `string` for the two product fields, and `number[]` for the two lists of scores, as the bubbles show. So `label.toUpperCase()` and `Math.max(...moreQuizzes)` both type-check. Had you typed the parameters as `{ length: number }` instead, each result would be only `{ length: number }`, and neither call would compile. Both arguments share one `T`, so they must be the same kind of value: a string and an array in one call is a type error.

examples.title: Find by id
examples.prompt: Find a product and a customer with one generic `byId`, and get back the full type of each.
examples.explanation: The constraint is all the body needs: it lets the callback read `item.id`. A constraint is a minimum, not an exact shape, so `Product` and `Customer` both fit even though they have more than an `id`. Because the result is `T`, searching products returns `Product | undefined` and searching customers returns `Customer | undefined`, so `name`, `priceCents`, and `email` are all there to use. `find` returns `undefined` when nothing matches, as the return type says, so each call handles that with a check, `?.`, or `??`.

examples.title: Breaking the constraint
examples.prompt: Pass `byId` a list whose items have no `id`, and read the error.
examples.output:
main.ts(6,18): error TS2345: Argument of type '{ label: string; }[]' is not assignable to parameter of type 'readonly { id: string; }[]'.
  Property 'id' is missing in type '{ label: string; }' but required in type '{ id: string; }'.

practice.title: Sort by name
practice.prompt:
Make `sortByName` generic, so it sorts any list of objects that have a `name` and keeps their type.

1. Give `sortByName` a type parameter `T` that extends `{ name: string }`, the parameter `xs: readonly T[]`, and the return type `T[]`.
2. Return a sorted copy of `xs` made with `toSorted`, comparing names with `localeCompare`.
3. Print the sorted products as `<name>: $<price>`, with the price in dollars to 2 decimals.
4. Keep the `export`: hidden type tests import `sortByName`, and Check also sorts another list.

Expected output:

```text
Ana (design)
Ben (sales)
Caro (support)
Kettle: $34.50
Mug: $12.99
Teapot: $21.00
```

tests.output:
Ana (design)
Ben (sales)
Caro (support)
Kettle: $34.50
Mug: $12.99
Teapot: $21.00

tests.harness:
{{code}}
console.log(sortByName([{ name: "Zoe", seat: 2 }, { name: "Eli", seat: 7 }]).map((g) => `${g.name} in seat ${g.seat}`).join(", "));
tests.output:
Ana (design)
Ben (sales)
Caro (support)
Kettle: $34.50
Mug: $12.99
Teapot: $21.00
Eli in seat 7, Zoe in seat 2

cases.name: keeps the items' own type
cases.code: const s: { name: string; age: number }[] = sortByName([{ name: "a", age: 1 }]);

hints: Follow `byId` from the examples: declare `<T extends { name: string }>`, then write `T` wherever the signature says `Employee`.
`toSorted` returns a sorted copy and leaves `xs` alone. Its callback compares two items: `(a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name)`.
Print the products in a second loop, like the employees, with `p.name` and `(p.priceCents / 100).toFixed(2)` in a template string.

steps.title: keyof and indexed access

examples.title: Keys as a type
examples.prompt: Derive a type for `User`'s keys and one for its `email` property, then use them to print some fields.
examples.output:
name: Ada
email: ada@example.com
Contact: ada@example.com

examples.title: Look up one property
examples.prompt: Read two properties of a user with a generic `getProp`, and get each one back with its own type.

examples.title: Pluck a column
examples.prompt: Collect one property from every order with a generic `pluck`, for a string property and a number property.
examples.output:
o1, o2, o3
Largest: 4500 cents
Customers: Ada, Ben, Ada
examples.explanation: `T[K][]` reads as an array of `T[K]`: one value of the picked property per item. With `"id"` that's a `string[]`, and with `"totalCents"` it's a `number[]`, which `Math.max(...totals)` accepts. Inside, `x[key]` is typed `T[K]` as well, so `map` returns exactly the declared type with no annotations in the body. The values come back in the order of the items, duplicates included, which is why Ada appears twice.

practice.title: Column
practice.prompt:
Make `column` generic, so it collects one property from every row with that property's type.

1. Give `column` the type parameters `T` and `K extends keyof T`, the parameters `rows: readonly T[]` and `key: K`, and the return type `T[K][]`.
2. Return the value under `key` for every row, in order.
3. Print the product names joined with `, `, then `Total: $` and the sum of the `priceCents` column in dollars to 2 decimals.
4. Keep the `export`s: hidden type tests import `column` and `products`, and Check also reads other columns.

Expected output:

```text
Mug, Kettle, Teapot
Total: $67.49
```

tests.output:
Mug, Kettle, Teapot
Total: $67.49
MUG-01 KET-02 TEA-03
1 5

cases.name: rejects a column products don't have

hints: The signature is `pluck`'s from the examples, with `rows` in place of `xs`.
`rows.map((row) => row[key])` returns one value per row, and `row[key]` is already typed `T[K]`.
Add up the prices with `column(products, "priceCents").reduce((sum, cents) => sum + cents, 0)`, then print the sum divided by 100 with `toFixed(2)`.

steps.title: Const, NoInfer, and overloads

examples.title: Const type parameter
examples.prompt: Declare a site's routes once, keep their exact paths in the type, and only allow links to those paths.

examples.title: NoInfer
examples.prompt: Create a state machine whose starting state must be one of its states, then start it in a state it doesn't have.
examples.output: main.ts(5,62): error TS2345: Argument of type '"paused"' is not assignable to parameter of type '"idle" | "playing" | "stopped"'.

examples.title: Overloads or keyof
examples.prompt: Read typed settings by key twice: with overloads, one per key, and with one generic signature on `keyof`.
examples.explanation: The first two `getSetting` lines have no body: they are overload signatures, the calls callers may make. The third is the implementation. Callers never see its signature, and it must accept the arguments of every overload. Each overload has its own return type, so `port` is a `number`. But every new key needs another overload, and `debug` has none, so `getSetting("debug")` fails with TS2769, `No overload matches this call`. The generic `setting` covers every key of `Settings` with one signature, and a key added to `Settings` works with no change to the function. Keep overloads for calls that differ in shape, like a different number of parameters.

practice.title: Select menu
practice.prompt:
Make `select` keep each menu's exact options, and reject a starting choice that isn't one of them.

1. Give `select` a `const` type parameter `T` that extends `readonly string[]`, and type `options` as `T`.
2. Type `initial` as `NoInfer<T[number]>`, the union of the options that `options` alone decides.
3. Give `select` the return type `{ options: T; selected: T[number] }`.
4. Print a color menu with the options red, green, and blue, starting on green, the same way as the size menu.
5. Keep the `export`: hidden type tests import `select`, and Check also builds other menus.

Expected output:

```text
Size: m of s, m, l
Color: green of red, green, blue
```

tests.output:
Size: m of s, m, l
Color: green of red, green, blue

Size: m of s, m, l
Color: green of red, green, blue
Drink: coffee of tea, coffee

cases.name: rejects a choice that isn't an option
keeps the options as a tuple

hints: Start from `routes` in the first example: `<const T extends readonly string[]>` and `options: T`.
`T[number]` is the type of one element of `T`, here the union of the options. Wrapped as `NoInfer<T[number]>`, it can't add a new option.
The whole signature is `export function select<const T extends readonly string[]>(options: T, initial: NoInfer<T[number]>): { options: T; selected: T[number] }`.

recap:
- `T extends { id: string }` constrains a type parameter: the body can use `id`, and callers still get their full type back.
- A constraint is a minimum. Types with more members fit, and types without the member are rejected at the call.
- `keyof T` is the union of `T`'s keys, and `T[K]` is the type stored under the key `K`.
- `<T, K extends keyof T>` with a return type of `T[K]` types a lookup exactly, and rejects keys the type doesn't have.
- `<const T>` keeps the literal types of an argument written in the call, as if it had `as const`.
- `NoInfer<S>` stops a parameter from helping infer `S`, so it is only checked against what the other arguments decided.
- Overloads list several signatures for one function. When the result is a lookup by key, one generic signature on `keyof` scales better.
